title: The roots: Abraham and the people of Israel
text:
Every big tree has roots hidden under the ground. Christianity is like a tree, and its roots go back almost 4,000 years, long before Jesus was born.

The story starts with a man called Abraham. He lived in the Middle East, in a land that today is Iraq. The [Bible] says that God asked Abraham to leave his home and travel to a new country, called [Canaan]. Abraham trusted God and went, with his wife Sarah, his tents, his sheep and his camels.

God made Abraham a [promise]: his family would become a great people, as many as the stars in the sky. That family became the people of Israel, also called the Hebrews and later the Jews.

Many years later, the Hebrews became slaves in Egypt. The Bible tells how a leader named [Moses] led them out of Egypt. On a mountain, Moses received the [Ten Commandments], ten simple rules like "Do not steal" and "Honour your father and your mother".

The people of Israel believed in only one God. This was quite rare at the time, because most nations around them prayed to many gods: a god of the sun, a god of rain, a god of war...

Over hundreds of years, the Jews wrote down their history, their laws, their songs and their poems. These writings became the [Hebrew Bible]. Christians call it the [Old Testament], and it is the first and biggest part of the Christian Bible.

In the Hebrew Bible, special messengers called [prophets] said that one day God would send a [Messiah], a saviour who would bring peace and justice to the world.

Jesus was born into this Jewish people. He read these same scriptures, prayed these same prayers and went to the same Temple. So to understand Christianity, you have to start with Abraham, Moses and the Jewish people. That is why Jews, Christians and Muslims are sometimes called the "children of Abraham".

title: Jesus is born in Bethlehem
text:
About 2,000 years ago, a baby was born who would change the history of the world. His name was Jesus.

At that time, the land of Israel was ruled by the powerful [Roman Empire]. The Roman emperor, Augustus, ordered a big [census], a counting of all the people. So a young woman called Mary and her husband Joseph, a carpenter, had to travel from their village of Nazareth to the small town of [Bethlehem].

The town was full of travellers, and there was no room for them at the inn. So Mary gave birth to her baby in a place where animals were kept, and she laid him in a [manger], a feeding box for animals.

The [Gospels], the books that tell the life of Jesus, say that angels appeared to shepherds in the fields at night. The angels sang and told them the good news. The shepherds hurried to see the baby.

Later, wise men called the [Magi] came from the East. They had followed a bright star. They brought gifts: gold, frankincense (a perfume that smells nice when burned) and myrrh (a precious oil).

But the local king, [Herod], was jealous. He was afraid this baby would take his throne. So Joseph, Mary and Jesus ran away to Egypt for a while, until it was safe to come back.

Jesus grew up in Nazareth. He probably learned to be a carpenter like Joseph. He spoke [Aramaic], and he went to the synagogue to learn the Jewish scriptures.

Fun fact: we count our years from the birth of Jesus! "AD" means "Anno Domini", in the year of the Lord. But a monk who did the maths 500 years later made a small mistake, so Jesus was probably born around the year 4 BC, a few years "before Christ"!

Today, Christians all over the world celebrate the birth of Jesus at [Christmas], on the 25th of December (or on the 7th of January in many [Orthodox] churches).

title: John the Baptist baptizes Jesus
text:
When Jesus was about 30 years old, something important happened near the Jordan River.

A man named John was living in the desert. He wore clothes made of camel hair and ate locusts (a kind of grasshopper) and wild honey. People called him John the Baptist.

John was a [prophet]. He told people: "Change your hearts! Stop doing bad things, share with the poor, be honest!" Many people came to listen to him.

To show that they wanted to start a new life, people went into the river, and John poured water on them or dipped them under the water. This was called [baptism]. The water was a sign of being washed clean on the inside, not just on the outside.

One day, Jesus came to the river and asked John to baptize him. John was surprised. He said: "I should be baptized by you, not the other way round!" But Jesus insisted.

The Gospels say that when Jesus came out of the water, the sky opened, and the [Holy Spirit] came down on him like a dove. A voice from heaven said: "This is my beloved Son, with whom I am well pleased."

After his baptism, Jesus went into the desert for 40 days to pray and fast (to go without food). The Gospels say he was tempted by the [devil], but he refused to do wrong.

This moment is the beginning of Jesus' [ministry], the few years when he travelled and taught people.

Baptism became the first and most important sign of being a Christian. Even today, when someone becomes a Christian, they are baptized with water, sometimes as a baby, sometimes as a grown-up. In some churches people are dipped completely under the water, like in the Jordan River. In others, a little water is poured on the head.

That is why the dove is a symbol of the Holy Spirit and of peace in Christian art.

title: Jesus teaches, heals and chooses twelve friends
text:
For about three years, Jesus walked from village to village in [Galilee], a green region around a big lake called the Sea of Galilee.

He chose twelve close friends to follow him. They were called the [disciples] and later the [apostles]. Some of them were fishermen, like Peter and his brother Andrew, and James and John. Jesus told them: "Follow me, and I will make you fishers of people!"

Jesus was a great storyteller. He taught with short stories called [parables]. In one of them, a shepherd leaves his 99 sheep to look for the one lost sheep. In another, a man called the [Good Samaritan] helps a wounded stranger, even though their peoples didn't like each other. The message: everyone is your neighbour!

On a hill, Jesus gave a famous speech called the Sermon on the Mount. He said: "Blessed are the peacemakers", "Love your enemies", and "Treat others the way you want to be treated." He also taught his friends a prayer, the "Our Father" (or [Lord's Prayer]), which Christians still say every day.

The Gospels also tell about [miracles]: Jesus healed blind and sick people, calmed a storm, and fed 5,000 people with just five loaves of bread and two fish.

Jesus liked to spend time with people others ignored: poor people, sick people, children, and even tax collectors, whom everybody hated. When his disciples tried to send children away, Jesus said: "Let the children come to me!"

Not everyone was happy. Some religious leaders thought Jesus was breaking the rules, for example by healing people on the [Sabbath], the day of rest. And the Romans didn't like anyone who attracted big crowds.

Many people began to wonder: is Jesus the [Messiah] promised by the prophets? Peter answered: "You are the Christ!" "Christ" is the Greek word for Messiah. That's where the word "Christian" comes from.

title: The Last Supper, the cross and Easter morning
text:
This is the most important moment for Christians, and it happened in just a few days.

Jesus and his disciples went to [Jerusalem] for the Jewish festival of [Passover]. When Jesus rode into the city on a donkey, crowds waved palm branches and shouted "Hosanna!" Christians remember this day as [Palm Sunday].

A few days later, Jesus had a last meal with his twelve friends: the Last Supper. He took bread, broke it and said: "This is my body." He took a cup of wine and said: "This is my blood." He asked them to repeat this meal to remember him. This became the [Eucharist], also called Holy Communion or the Lord's Supper, which Christians still share today.

That night, one of the disciples, Judas, betrayed Jesus for 30 silver coins. Jesus was arrested in a garden. Peter, afraid, said three times that he didn't know him.

The religious leaders accused Jesus of claiming to be the Son of God. They brought him to the Roman governor, [Pontius Pilate]. Pilate did not find him guilty, but he was afraid of the crowd, so he sentenced Jesus to [crucifixion]. This was the cruel way the Romans punished criminals: they were nailed to a wooden cross. Jesus died on a Friday, which Christians call [Good Friday].

His friends put his body in a tomb carved in the rock, and closed it with a big stone.

But on Sunday morning, some women, including [Mary Magdalene], came to the tomb. The stone was rolled away, and the tomb was empty! The Gospels say that Jesus appeared to them, alive. Then he appeared to the disciples many times.

This is called the [Resurrection]. Christians believe that Jesus beat death, and that this opens the way to [eternal life] for everyone. They celebrate it every year at [Easter], the most important Christian feast. That's why the cross, once a sign of shame, became the sign of Christianity.

title: Pentecost: the Church is born
text:
After his resurrection, the Gospels say that Jesus stayed with his disciples for 40 days. Then he went up to heaven. This is called the [Ascension]. Before leaving, he told them: "Go into the whole world and tell the good news to everyone!"

But the disciples were scared. They stayed hidden in a room in Jerusalem, praying with Mary, Jesus' mother.

Ten days later, on the Jewish festival of [Pentecost], something amazing happened. The Book of [Acts] says there was a noise like a strong wind, and little flames like tongues of fire appeared above each of them. They were filled with the [Holy Spirit].

Suddenly, the frightened disciples became brave! They went out into the street and started speaking to the crowd. Jerusalem was full of visitors from many countries, and each person heard them speaking in his own language! Some people laughed and said: "They're drunk!" But Peter stood up and said: "No, it's only nine in the morning!"

Then Peter gave his first big speech about Jesus. That day, about 3,000 people were baptized. This is why Pentecost is often called the "birthday of the Church".

The first Christians lived like a big family. The Book of Acts says they shared everything they had, so that nobody was poor. They prayed together, ate together, and "broke bread" at home to remember Jesus.

At first, all the Christians were Jews. They still went to the [Temple] to pray. They saw Jesus as the Messiah promised to Israel.

The leaders of this first community were the apostles, especially [Peter], whom Jesus had called "the rock", and James, a relative of Jesus.

Today, Christians still celebrate Pentecost 50 days after Easter. "Pentecost" comes from a Greek word meaning "fiftieth".

title: Stephen the first martyr, and Saul on the road to Damascus
text:
The new group of Jesus' followers was growing fast, and that made some people angry.

One of the first Christian helpers was a young man called Stephen. His job was to give food to widows and poor people. He was also a brilliant speaker. Some leaders accused him of speaking against God and the Temple. They took him out of the city and threw stones at him until he died. Before dying, Stephen prayed: "Lord, do not hold this sin against them." He forgave them, like Jesus did on the cross.

Stephen became the first Christian [martyr]. A martyr is someone who dies because they refuse to give up their faith.

Watching the stoning, and approving it, was a young man named Saul. Saul was a very clever and very strict Jew, from the city of Tarsus. He was a [Pharisee], and he was sure the Christians were dangerous. He started to hunt them down and put them in prison.

One day, Saul was travelling to the city of [Damascus] to arrest more Christians. Suddenly, a blinding light from the sky flashed around him. He fell to the ground and heard a voice: "Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting me?" Saul asked: "Who are you, Lord?" The voice answered: "I am Jesus."

When Saul got up, he was blind! His companions led him by the hand into Damascus. For three days, he didn't eat or drink. Then a Christian named Ananias came, even though he was afraid of Saul. He laid his hands on him, and something like scales fell from Saul's eyes. He could see again!

Saul was baptized. The enemy of the Christians became one of the greatest Christians of all time. He started using his Roman name, Paul.

Today, when someone changes their mind completely, people sometimes say they had a "road to Damascus" moment. This change of heart is called a [conversion].

title: Paul's great journeys and letters
text:
After his conversion, Paul became a super-traveller! He wanted everyone, not only Jews, to hear about Jesus.

In the city of [Antioch], in today's Turkey, the followers of Jesus were called "Christians" for the very first time. From there, Paul set off on long [missionary journeys]. In about ten years, he travelled more than 15,000 kilometres, on foot and by boat, across today's Turkey, Greece and Cyprus.

His adventures were incredible! He was shipwrecked three times. Once, he spent a whole night and a day floating in the open sea. He was beaten, thrown in prison, and once his friends had to help him escape from a city by lowering him over the wall in a basket! In prison with his friend Silas, he sang songs at midnight, and an earthquake opened the prison doors.

A big question came up: do non-Jews, called [Gentiles], have to follow all the Jewish laws to become Christians? In about the year 49, the apostles met in Jerusalem to discuss it. They decided: no, Gentiles can become Christians without becoming Jews first. This opened the door for Christianity to spread across the whole world.

Paul founded small churches in many cities: Philippi, Thessalonica, Corinth, Ephesus... A "church" at that time was not a building. It was a group of people meeting in someone's house.

When Paul was far away, he wrote letters to these churches to encourage them and answer their questions. These letters are called [epistles]. Thirteen of them are in the [New Testament]. They are the oldest Christian writings we have, even older than the Gospels!

In one famous letter, Paul wrote: "Love is patient, love is kind. It is not jealous, it does not boast... Love never fails." These words are often read at weddings today.

At the end, Paul was arrested and, as a Roman citizen, he asked to be judged in Rome by the emperor himself.

title: The fire of Rome: Peter and Paul die for their faith
text:
By the year 60, there was already a Christian community in [Rome], the capital of the huge Roman Empire. Both Peter and Paul had come there.

In July of the year 64, a terrible fire broke out in Rome. It burned for six days. A big part of the city was destroyed, and many people lost their homes.

The emperor at the time was [Nero]. He was not a nice emperor! Many Romans suspected that Nero himself had started the fire, because he wanted to build a gigantic new palace, the "Golden House". There is even a legend that he played music while the city burned (but this is probably not true).

To make people stop blaming him, Nero needed someone else to blame. He chose the Christians. They were a small, strange group to most Romans: they refused to worship the Roman gods and the emperor, and they met in secret. Rumours said they were enemies of everybody.

So Nero started the first big [persecution] of Christians. A Roman historian named [Tacitus] wrote about it. Many Christians were arrested and killed in cruel ways, in front of crowds.

According to very old Christian tradition, both Peter and Paul died in Rome at around this time. Paul, as a Roman citizen, had his head cut off with a sword, which was considered a "quicker" death. Peter was crucified. The tradition says he asked to be crucified upside down, because he did not feel worthy to die in the same way as Jesus.

Peter was buried on a hill called the Vatican. Many years later, a huge church was built over his tomb: [Saint Peter's Basilica], the biggest church in the world.

Because Peter was the leader of the apostles and died in Rome, the bishops of Rome, later called the [popes], were seen as his successors.

Instead of destroying the Christians, persecution made them stronger. A Christian writer later said: "The blood of martyrs is the seed of the Church."

title: The Temple is destroyed and the Gospels are written
text:
In the year 66, the Jews of Judea rebelled against the Romans, who ruled their land. The Romans sent a big army. In the year 70, the Roman general Titus surrounded [Jerusalem], captured it and burned the magnificent [Temple].

The Temple was the most sacred place for the Jews. Only one wall of the courtyard still stands today: the [Western Wall] in Jerusalem, where Jews still come to pray. In Rome, you can still see the Arch of Titus, which shows Roman soldiers carrying away the Temple's golden candlestick, the menorah.

This was a huge change for both Jews and Christians. Little by little, the Jewish followers of Jesus and the other Jews went separate ways. Christianity became a religion of its own, with more and more non-Jewish members.

At the same time, the people who had known Jesus personally were getting old and dying. The Christians realized: we must write down everything about Jesus before it is forgotten!

So, between about the years 65 and 100, four books about the life of Jesus were written. They are called the [Gospels], which means "good news". They are named after Mark, Matthew, Luke and John. Mark is probably the oldest and the shortest. Luke also wrote a second book, the [Acts of the Apostles], about the first Christians.

Each Gospel tells the story from its own angle, a bit like four friends describing the same football match. That's why there are small differences between them.

They were written in Greek, the language that most people in the eastern Roman Empire understood, a bit like English today.

Together with Paul's letters and a few other writings, the Gospels form the [New Testament]. The final book, called [Revelation], is full of strange visions of angels, dragons and a new Jerusalem at the end of time.

The Old Testament and the New Testament together make up the Christian [Bible]. Today it is the most translated book in the world, in more than 700 languages!

title: Secret signs and the catacombs
text:
What was it like to be a Christian in the Roman Empire, around the year 150? Let's imagine!

Being a Christian was not exactly forbidden everywhere all the time, but it could be dangerous. If a neighbour reported you, you could be arrested. So Christians were often careful.

They used secret signs. The most famous is the fish! In Greek, "fish" is written [ΙΧΘΥΣ::The Greek word "ichthys", which means fish. Christians used it as a secret code: each letter is the first letter of the words "Jesus Christ, God's Son, Saviour" in Greek.] (ichthys). The letters are the first letters of "Jesus Christ, Son of God, Saviour". A legend says that when two strangers met, one would draw half a fish in the sand. If the other finished the drawing, they knew they were both Christians!

Christians did not have churches yet. They met on Sunday, the day of the resurrection, very early in the morning, in someone's house. A writer named Justin Martyr described a Sunday meeting: they read the "memories of the apostles" (the Gospels) and the prophets, someone gave a talk, they prayed together, and they shared bread and wine, the Eucharist. Then they collected money for orphans, widows, sick people and prisoners.

In Rome, Christians buried their dead in [catacombs]. These are long underground tunnels dug in the soft rock outside the city, sometimes on four levels, with hundreds of kilometres of corridors! The Romans usually burned their dead, but Christians preferred to bury them, because they believed in the resurrection of the body.

On the walls of the catacombs, Christians painted pictures: Jesus as the [Good Shepherd] carrying a lamb on his shoulders, Noah's ark, Jonah and the big fish, a dove, an anchor (a symbol of hope)...

Contrary to a popular legend, Christians did not live hidden in the catacombs. They went there for funerals and to remember the martyrs.

What made Christians special for the Romans was how they cared for others. A Roman emperor later complained: "These Christians feed not only their own poor, but ours too!"

title: Perpetua and Felicity, brave young martyrs
text:
In the year 203, in the city of [Carthage] in North Africa (today's Tunisia), there lived a young woman called Perpetua. She was 22 years old, from a rich family, and she had a little baby boy.

Perpetua was learning about Christianity to be baptized. At that time, the emperor Septimius Severus had forbidden people to become Christians. Perpetua was arrested together with her slave, Felicity, who was expecting a baby, and a few other young Christians.

What makes this story special is that Perpetua kept a diary in prison! It is one of the very first texts written by a Christian woman that we still have today. She wrote about the dark, hot prison, about how worried she was for her baby, and about her dreams.

Her father, who was not a Christian, came to see her many times. He cried and begged her: "Just say you are not a Christian! Think of your son!" Perpetua pointed at a water jug and asked him: "Can this jug be called by any other name than what it is?" "No," said her father. "Neither can I be called anything other than what I am: a Christian."

In prison, Felicity gave birth to a baby girl, who was adopted by a Christian family.

On the emperor's birthday, the prisoners were taken to the [amphitheatre], a big stadium where the Romans watched games. They were thrown to wild animals: a leopard, a bear, a wild cow. The story says that Perpetua and Felicity held each other's hands and stood up together, bravely. Finally, they were killed by soldiers.

The story of their courage was read aloud in churches for centuries. In North Africa, it was so popular that a bishop had to remind people that it was not part of the Bible!

Perpetua and Felicity are remembered as [saints]. Their story shows that, from the very beginning, women played an important role in the Church. Their feast day is the 7th of March.

title: Anthony goes into the desert: the first monks
text:
Around the year 270, in Egypt, a young man named Anthony went to church and heard a sentence from the Gospel: "If you want to be perfect, go, sell what you have and give to the poor, and come, follow me."

Anthony felt that Jesus was speaking directly to him. He was about 20 years old and his parents had died, leaving him a big farm. So he did exactly that! He sold everything, gave the money to the poor, and went to live alone in the desert.

There, he prayed, fasted, worked with his hands making baskets, and read the Bible. He lived in an old tomb, and later in an abandoned fort, and finally in a cave on a mountain near the Red Sea. His life was very simple: a little bread, salt and water.

The stories say that he fought against [demons] who tried to scare him or tempt him. But he stayed calm and trusted God.

Anthony lived to be 105 years old! Even though he wanted to be alone, many people came to see him to ask for advice. Many others decided to live like him. Soon, thousands of men and women were living in the Egyptian desert. They were called the Desert Fathers and Desert Mothers. They are the first [monks] and [nuns].

The word "monk" comes from a Greek word meaning "alone". Some monks lived completely alone, as [hermits]. Others, following a man named Pachomius, lived together in groups, in a [monastery], where they prayed and worked together, with rules and a leader.

The Desert Fathers left many wise sayings. One of them said: "If you see a young monk climbing up to heaven by his own will, grab him by the foot and pull him down, because it is not good for him!" In other words: don't show off!

This idea of monks and monasteries spread everywhere in the Christian world. For more than a thousand years, monasteries were among the most important places for prayer, learning, farming and helping the poor.

title: The Great Persecution under Diocletian
text:
By the year 300, around one person out of ten in the Roman Empire was a Christian. There were churches in many cities, and Christians even worked in the emperor's palace and in the army.

But the emperor Diocletian was worried. The empire had lots of problems: wars on the borders, money troubles, and too many generals who wanted to become emperor. Diocletian thought that if everyone went back to worshipping the old Roman gods, the gods would protect Rome again. The Christians, who refused, looked like troublemakers to him.

In the year 303, Diocletian started what is called the Great Persecution. It was the worst and longest one in history. He gave orders to:
- destroy churches,
- burn all copies of the Christian scriptures,
- remove Christians from important jobs,
- arrest the priests and bishops,
- force everybody to offer a [sacrifice] to the gods, or be punished.

Many Christians were put in prison, sent to work in mines, tortured or killed. Some gave in and made the sacrifice to save their lives. Others hid their Bibles in secret places. Many stood firm.

Some of the most famous [saints] come from this time. Saint George, the soldier who, in the legend, fights a dragon, was probably a Roman soldier killed during this persecution. Saint Agnes, a young girl in Rome, is another one.

In the east of the empire, the persecution lasted almost ten years. In the west, it was shorter, because the ruler there, Constantius, did not really enforce the orders. His son had a name you will see on the next pin: Constantine!

In the end, the persecution failed. There were simply too many Christians, and many Romans admired their courage. In 311, one of the emperors, Galerius, gave up, and signed a law allowing Christians to exist, asking them to pray for him. The age of the martyrs was coming to an end.

title: Constantine and the Edict of Milan: freedom for Christians
text:
In the year 312, two men were fighting to become emperor of Rome: Constantine and Maxentius. Their armies met near a bridge over the River Tiber, called the Milvian Bridge.

The night before the battle, the story says that Constantine saw a sign in the sky, or in a dream. It was a cross, or the letters [☧::The Chi-Rho: the first two letters of the word "Christ" in Greek, X (chi) and P (rho), placed one on top of the other. Constantine put it on his soldiers' shields.] and the words: "In this sign, you will conquer!" He ordered his soldiers to paint this Christian sign on their shields.

Constantine won the battle, and Maxentius drowned in the river. Constantine became the master of the western part of the empire. He believed that the God of the Christians had given him victory.

In the year 313, Constantine and the eastern emperor Licinius met in the city of Milan. They signed an agreement known as the Edict of Milan. It said that everybody in the empire was free to follow the religion of his choice, including Christianity! The Christians got back their churches and the things that had been taken from them.

What a change! Just ten years earlier, Christians were being thrown in prison. Now, the emperor himself was on their side.

Constantine gave money to build big churches, like the first Saint Peter's Basilica in Rome. His mother, [Helena], travelled to Jerusalem and had churches built at the places where Jesus was born, died and rose from the dead, like the Church of the Holy Sepulchre.

He also made Sunday an official day of rest in the whole empire, in the year 321. So if you don't go to school on Sunday, you can thank Constantine!

In 330, he founded a new capital in the east and gave it his name: [Constantinople] (today Istanbul, in Turkey).

Constantine was baptized only on his deathbed, in 337. Some historians think he was sincerely a believer; others think he also used religion for politics. Probably both are true!

title: The Council of Nicaea and the Creed
text:
Now that Christians were free, they could finally meet openly. But they discovered that they didn't all agree about everything!

A big argument started in Egypt. A priest from Alexandria named [Arius] taught that Jesus, the Son of God, was very great, but not truly God like the Father. He said God created the Son, so "there was a time when the Son did not exist." Others, like the young deacon [Athanasius], said: "No! Jesus is truly God, just as much as the Father."

This might sound like a complicated question, but for Christians it was very important. Everybody was arguing about it, even in the markets! A writer joked that if you asked a baker the price of bread, he would answer: "The Father is greater than the Son!"

Emperor Constantine wanted peace and unity in his empire. So in the year 325, he invited all the bishops to the city of [Nicaea] (in today's Turkey). About 300 bishops came, some with scars from the persecutions. It was the first [ecumenical council], which means a meeting of the whole Church.

After long discussions, the bishops decided that Jesus is "of the same substance" as the Father: he is truly God. They wrote a short text summing up the Christian faith: the [Creed], a word that comes from the Latin "credo", meaning "I believe". A slightly longer version was finished in 381 and is called the [Nicene Creed]. It starts: "I believe in one God, the Father Almighty, maker of heaven and earth..."

This Creed is still said today in Catholic, Orthodox, Anglican, Lutheran and many other churches. It explains the idea of the [Trinity]: one God in three persons, the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit.

The Council also decided how to calculate the date of Easter every year: the first Sunday after the first full moon of spring. That's why Easter is on a different date each year!

In 2025, Christians celebrated the 1,700th anniversary of this council.

title: Christianity becomes the religion of the Empire
text:
After Constantine, almost all the emperors were Christians. But until then, the old Roman gods, like Jupiter and Venus, still had their temples and their priests.

In the year 380, the emperor Theodosius made a big decision. With a law called the Edict of Thessalonica, he declared that Christianity, as described in the Creed of Nicaea, was the official religion of the Roman Empire.

A few years later, he went further: he forbade sacrifices to the old gods, and many pagan temples were closed. The famous [Olympic Games], which were linked to the Greek god Zeus, stopped a few years later too.

In just 70 years, everything was turned upside down. Christianity went from being a persecuted religion to being the religion of the emperor! Sadly, some Christians then started persecuting others, like the followers of the old religions, or Christians who didn't think the same way. Power can be dangerous...

But even an emperor could be told off! A famous story: in 390, in the city of Thessalonica, a crowd killed a Roman officer. Theodosius was furious and ordered his soldiers to punish the city. Thousands of innocent people were killed.

The bishop of Milan, [Ambrose], was horrified. When the emperor came to church, Ambrose stopped him at the door and said: "You cannot come in until you have done [penance] for this crime!" And the most powerful man in the world obeyed. He took off his royal robes and publicly asked God for forgiveness.

This was an important moment: it showed that even an emperor was not above God's law.

Theodosius was the last emperor to rule over the whole Roman Empire. When he died in 395, the empire was divided between his two sons: the Western Empire, with Rome, and the Eastern Empire, with Constantinople. This division would become very important for the history of the Church.

title: Two great teachers: Jerome and Augustine
text:
Around the year 400, two men wrote books that shaped Christianity for more than a thousand years.

The first one was Jerome. He was a scholar who loved books and had a bad temper! He learned Hebrew, which was very rare for a Christian at the time, and went to live in a cave in Bethlehem, near the place where Jesus was born.

The Pope asked him to make a good translation of the Bible into [Latin], the language spoken in the western part of the Roman Empire. Jerome worked on it for more than 20 years. His translation is called the [Vulgate], which means "for the common people". It was THE Bible of Western Europe for over 1,000 years.

In paintings, Jerome is often shown with a lion. The legend says he took a thorn out of a lion's paw, and the lion stayed with him as a friend!

The second man was Augustine. He was born in North Africa, in today's Algeria. His mother, Monica, was a Christian, but Augustine was not interested at all. As a teenager, he stole pears from a neighbour's tree, just for fun, not even to eat them! He studied, became a famous teacher of speaking in public, and went to live in Milan.

For years, Augustine searched for the meaning of life. One day, in a garden, he heard a child's voice singing: "Take and read! Take and read!" He opened the Bible and read a sentence of Paul that changed his life. He was baptized by Bishop Ambrose.

Augustine went back to Africa and became the bishop of a city called Hippo. He wrote more than 100 books! In "[Confessions]", he told the story of his life, a bit like a long letter to God. One of his famous sentences is: "You made us for yourself, Lord, and our heart is restless until it rests in you."

His other big book, "The City of God", was written after the city of Rome was attacked by the [Visigoths] in 410. People were asking: "Is the world ending?" Augustine explained that earthly cities can fall, but God's city lasts forever.

title: Saint Patrick brings Christianity to Ireland
text:
Patrick was born around the year 385 in Roman Britain. His family was Christian, but young Patrick wasn't very interested in religion.

When he was 16 years old, something terrible happened. Pirates from Ireland attacked his village, captured him and took him across the sea as a slave! In Ireland, he had to look after sheep on a lonely mountain, in the cold and the rain, often hungry.

Alone with his sheep, Patrick started to pray, a hundred times a day, he said. His faith became very strong.

After six years, he had a dream telling him that a ship was waiting for him. He escaped, walked about 300 kilometres to the coast, and found a ship that took him home. What an adventure!

But back home, Patrick had another dream. He saw a man bringing letters from Ireland, and he heard the Irish people calling: "Please, holy boy, come and walk among us again!"

So Patrick studied to become a priest, and later a bishop. Around the year 432, he went back to Ireland, the land where he had been a slave, to tell the Irish about Jesus. That takes courage and forgiveness!

At that time, Ireland had never been part of the Roman Empire. The Irish followed [druids], the priests of the old Celtic religion. Patrick travelled all over the island, baptized thousands of people, and founded churches and monasteries.

A famous legend says that Patrick used a little three-leafed plant, the [shamrock], to explain the Trinity: three leaves, but only one plant, just like one God in three persons. Another legend says he chased all the snakes out of Ireland (but actually, there were no snakes in Ireland anyway, since the Ice Age!).

Patrick wrote a short book about his life, called the "[Confession::Patrick's own short book about his life. In it he tells how he was a slave, how he escaped, and why he came back to Ireland. It is one of the few texts we have written by Patrick himself.]", which we can still read today.

Thanks to Patrick, Ireland became a land of monasteries and scholars, called "the island of saints and scholars". Today, [Saint Patrick's Day], on the 17th of March, is celebrated all over the world with green clothes and parades!

title: The fall of Rome and the baptism of Clovis
text:
During the 400s, the Western Roman Empire became weaker and weaker. Peoples from the north and east, whom the Romans called "[barbarians]", crossed the borders: the Goths, the Vandals, the Franks, the Huns...

In the year 476, a Germanic chief removed the last Western emperor, a boy called Romulus Augustulus. Historians often use this date as the end of the Western Roman Empire, and the beginning of the [Middle Ages]. (The Eastern Empire, with Constantinople, continued for another thousand years!)

In this time of chaos, the Church was often the only organization that still worked. The bishops protected the cities, fed the poor and even negotiated with the invaders. Pope Leo the Great is said to have met Attila the Hun in 452 and convinced him not to attack Rome.

Many of these new peoples were already Christians, but they followed the ideas of Arius (remember the Council of Nicaea?). The [Franks], in the north of today's France and Belgium, were still [pagans].

The king of the Franks was a young and fierce warrior called Clovis. His wife, Queen Clotilde, was a Catholic Christian, and she kept asking him to become a Christian too. Clovis refused.

The story says that, during a hard battle against another people, the Alamanni, Clovis was losing. He prayed: "God of Clotilde, if you give me victory, I will believe in you!" And he won.

Around the year 496 (historians are not sure of the exact date), Clovis was baptized on Christmas Day in the city of Reims by the bishop Remigius, together with 3,000 of his soldiers! The bishop told him: "Bow your head, proud warrior. Burn what you have worshipped, and worship what you have burned."

This was very important: Clovis became the first great Catholic king of the barbarian kingdoms. The kingdom of the Franks later became France. For centuries, French kings were crowned in the cathedral of Reims, where Clovis was baptized, and France was called "the eldest daughter of the Church".

title: Saint Benedict: pray and work
text:
Benedict was born around the year 480 in Nursia, a small town in Italy. His parents sent him to Rome to study. But Benedict was shocked by the bad behaviour of the students there, who spent their time partying. So he left the city and went to live as a hermit in a cave in the mountains, at Subiaco.

For three years, he lived alone. A monk who lived nearby secretly brought him bread, lowering it down the rocks with a rope and a little bell!

Soon, other men heard about Benedict and wanted to live with him. Around the year 529, he founded a big monastery on top of a mountain between Rome and Naples: [Monte Cassino].

Benedict wrote a guidebook for his monks, called the Rule of Saint Benedict. It explained how to live together peacefully. It was wise and not too strict. Its motto can be summed up in three Latin words: "[Ora et labora]", which means "pray and work".

A monk's day was divided like a timetable:
- prayer and songs in the chapel, seven times a day, and once in the middle of the night,
- work in the fields, the kitchen or the workshop,
- reading and study,
- meals together, in silence, while someone read aloud,
- and sleep!

The monks promised to stay in the same monastery all their lives and to obey their leader, the [abbot], which means "father". They welcomed every guest "as if he were Christ himself".

Benedict's twin sister, Scholastica, founded a monastery for women nearby. A lovely story says that one evening, she wanted her brother to stay and talk longer. He refused. She prayed, and suddenly such a storm broke out that Benedict couldn't go home!

The Benedictine monasteries spread all over Europe. During the Middle Ages, they were like little islands of civilization: the monks farmed the land, made cheese and beer, took care of the sick, taught children, and copied ancient books by hand, saving many Latin and Greek texts from being lost forever.

That's why Benedict is the [patron saint] of Europe.

title: Hagia Sophia, the wonder of Constantinople
text:
While the West was in chaos, the Eastern Roman Empire, which historians call the [Byzantine Empire], was rich and powerful. Its capital, [Constantinople], was the biggest and most splendid city in the Christian world.

In the year 532, a huge riot broke out in Constantinople, starting at the chariot races. Half the city was burned, including the main church. The emperor [Justinian] decided to build a new church, the most beautiful the world had ever seen.

He called it Hagia Sophia, which means "Holy Wisdom" in Greek. Ten thousand workers built it in less than six years! It was finished in the year 537.

Its most amazing feature is its gigantic dome, 55 metres high, which seems to float in the air. At its base there are 40 windows, so the light comes in all around and makes the dome look like it is hanging from heaven. The walls were covered with coloured marble and golden [mosaics], pictures made of thousands of tiny pieces of glass and stone.

When Justinian entered it for the first time, he is supposed to have said: "Solomon, I have outdone you!" (King Solomon had built the first Temple in Jerusalem.)

For almost 1,000 years, Hagia Sophia was the largest church in the world. It was the heart of [Orthodox] Christianity, the kind of Christianity of the East.

Eastern Christians loved [icons]: paintings of Jesus, Mary and the saints on wooden panels, often with golden backgrounds. They don't pray to the picture itself, but the icon is like a window to heaven that helps them pray.

A legend says that when messengers from Russia visited Hagia Sophia centuries later, they said: "We didn't know whether we were in heaven or on earth!" (You'll meet them again on another pin.)

In 1453, Constantinople was conquered by the Ottoman Turks, and Hagia Sophia became a [mosque]. Later it became a museum, and since 2020 it is a mosque again. You can still visit it in Istanbul and see some of the old Christian mosaics.

title: Pope Gregory the Great sends monks to England
text:
Gregory was born in Rome around the year 540, in a rich and noble family. He became the mayor of Rome, but then he decided to give away his fortune, turned his family house into a monastery, and became a monk.

In 590, Rome was hit by floods and a terrible disease, the plague. The Pope died. The people chose Gregory as the new [pope]. He didn't want the job at all! A legend says he tried to escape the city hidden in a basket. But he was found and brought back.

Gregory turned out to be one of the greatest popes in history, which is why he is called Gregory "the Great". He organized food for the poor of Rome, negotiated with invaders, and wrote many books. He called himself "the servant of the servants of God", a title the popes still use today.

One day, before he was pope, Gregory saw some fair-haired boys being sold as slaves in the Roman market. He asked where they came from. "They are Angles," someone replied (the Angles were a people living in Britain). Gregory, who liked jokes, answered: "Not Angles, but angels!" The Angles were pagans, and Gregory decided that someday he would send them missionaries.

In 596, he sent a group of about 40 monks, led by a monk named [Augustine::Augustine of Canterbury, a monk from Rome sent by Pope Gregory to England. He became the first Archbishop of Canterbury. He is a different person from the famous Augustine of Hippo, who lived 200 years earlier in Africa.] (not the same as Augustine of Hippo!). They were very scared of the long journey and the fierce Anglo-Saxons, and almost gave up. Gregory wrote to them: "Keep going!"

In 597, they landed in Kent, in the south of England. King Æthelberht of Kent had a Christian wife, Bertha, and he welcomed them. He was soon baptized. Augustine became the first Archbishop of [Canterbury], which is still the main church of England today.

Gregory's name is also linked to a kind of music: [Gregorian chant]. It is a calm, beautiful singing, all together on a single melody, without instruments, in Latin. Monks still sing it today. It is one of the roots of all Western music!

title: Charlemagne and the monks who saved books
text:
On Christmas Day in the year 800, in Saint Peter's Basilica in Rome, something surprising happened. The king of the Franks, Charlemagne, was praying. Pope Leo III came up to him and placed a crown on his head. The crowd shouted: "Long live Charles, the great and peaceful emperor of the Romans!"

For the first time in over 300 years, there was an emperor in the West again. Charlemagne ruled a huge kingdom covering today's France, Germany, Belgium, the Netherlands, Switzerland, Austria and northern Italy.

Charlemagne was a great warrior, but also someone who loved learning, even though he himself struggled to write. He kept a writing tablet under his pillow to practise at night! He wanted his people to be educated and his priests to know how to read the Bible properly.

He invited the best scholars of Europe to his palace in Aachen, like an English monk named Alcuin. He ordered every monastery and cathedral to open a school. That's why a French legend says Charlemagne "invented school"!

In those days, there was no printing. Every book had to be copied by hand, letter by letter, by monks in a special room of the monastery called the [scriptorium]. Copying a whole Bible could take years! They wrote on [parchment], made from animal skin, with goose feather pens.

The most beautiful books were decorated with bright colours and gold. These are called [illuminated manuscripts]. The most famous one is the Book of Kells, made by Irish monks around the year 800. It contains the four Gospels, with incredible drawings of animals, knots and spirals. It is kept today in Dublin.

Charlemagne's scholars also created a new, clear and easy-to-read handwriting, called Carolingian minuscule. It is the ancestor of the lowercase letters you are reading right now!

Thanks to these monks, many ancient books, not only the Bible, but also Roman poems, history and science, were saved and passed down to us.

title: Cyril and Methodius create an alphabet for the Slavs
text:
In the 800s, Christianity had spread across most of Western Europe. But in the east, lived many peoples who were still pagans, like the [Slavs], the ancestors of today's Czechs, Slovaks, Poles, Serbs, Bulgarians, Ukrainians and Russians.

In the year 862, Prince Rastislav of Great Moravia (in today's Czech Republic and Slovakia) wrote to the emperor in Constantinople. He asked: "Please send us teachers who can explain the Christian faith to us in our own language!"

The emperor chose two brothers from the city of Thessalonica in Greece: Constantine (who later became a monk with the name Cyril) and Methodius. They had grown up near Slavic people, so they spoke their language.

But there was a problem: the Slavic language had no alphabet! Nobody had ever written it down. So Cyril did something amazing: he invented a completely new alphabet, specially designed for the sounds of the Slavic language. It is called the [Glagolitic] alphabet.

Then the two brothers translated the Gospels and the church prayers into Slavic. For the first time, the Slavs could hear Mass and read the Bible in their own language!

In 863 they arrived in Moravia. Not everyone was happy. Some German priests said that you could only pray to God in three languages: Hebrew, Greek and Latin, the three languages written on Jesus' cross. Cyril answered: "Doesn't the rain fall on everyone? Doesn't the sun shine on everyone?" He meant that God loves all peoples and all languages.

The Pope in Rome agreed with the two brothers and approved the Slavic liturgy. Cyril died in Rome in 869, and Methodius continued the work.

After their death, their students created another alphabet, simpler and based on Greek letters. They named it [Cyrillic] in honour of Cyril. Today, more than 250 million people use the Cyrillic alphabet, in Russia, Ukraine, Bulgaria, Serbia and elsewhere!

Cyril and Methodius are called the "apostles of the Slavs", and they are co-patrons of Europe with Saint Benedict.

title: Prince Vladimir and the baptism of Kyiv
text:
Around the year 1000, a big state called [Kievan Rus'] stretched across today's Ukraine, Belarus and western Russia. Its capital was Kyiv. Its prince, Vladimir, was a pagan warrior who worshipped many gods, like Perun, the god of thunder.

Vladimir's grandmother, Princess Olga, had become a Christian years before, but her son had refused to follow her.

An old chronicle tells a funny story. Vladimir wanted to choose a new religion for his people, so he sent messengers to visit different countries and see how they prayed.

The messengers went to visit Muslims, but Vladimir was not happy when he heard that they couldn't drink alcohol. "Drinking is the joy of the Rus'!" he said. They visited the Christians in Germany, but they found their churches not very beautiful.

Finally, they went to Constantinople, to the church of Hagia Sophia, during a big celebration with candles, incense, golden icons and magnificent singing. When they came back, they told Vladimir: "We didn't know whether we were in heaven or on earth! We only know that God lives there among people."

That convinced him. Of course, there were also political reasons: Vladimir wanted to marry Anna, the sister of the Byzantine emperor, and for that he had to become a Christian.

In the year 988, Vladimir was baptized. Then he ordered the statues of the old gods to be thrown into the river. He invited all the people of Kyiv to come to the [Dnieper] River. Priests from Constantinople baptized thousands of people at the same time, in the water!

Vladimir changed a lot after his baptism. He built churches and schools, and he took care of the poor, even sending carts of food through the city for those who were too sick to come.

That's how Christianity, in its Eastern [Orthodox] form, came to the peoples of Ukraine, Belarus and Russia. Today, Vladimir is honoured as a saint, and the Orthodox churches of these countries still love icons, onion-shaped domes and beautiful choirs.

title: The Great Schism: East and West separate
text:
Imagine two brothers who grow up in the same house, then move to different cities. They speak different languages, eat different food, and little by little they stop understanding each other. One day, they have a huge argument and stop talking. That's a bit what happened to the Christians of the East and the West.

In the West, around Rome, Christians spoke [Latin]. Their leader was the [Pope], the bishop of Rome. In the East, around Constantinople, they spoke Greek, and the most important bishop was the [Patriarch] of Constantinople.

Over the centuries, many differences appeared:
- In the West, priests had to be unmarried. In the East, they could be married.
- In the West, they used flat bread without yeast for communion. In the East, bread with yeast.
- They disagreed about a word added to the Creed in the West, "[filioque]", about the Holy Spirit.
- And above all: the Pope said he was the head of the whole Church. The Patriarch said the Pope was the "first among equals", but not the boss of everyone.

In the year 1054, the Pope sent a delegation to Constantinople, led by Cardinal Humbert, a man with a very bad temper. The discussions went badly. On the 16th of July, Humbert walked into Hagia Sophia during the service and put a paper on the altar: an [excommunication], which means throwing someone out of the Church. The Patriarch, Michael Cerularius, excommunicated them back!

At the time, people did not realize it was so serious. But from then on, the Church was divided in two: the [Catholic] Church in the West and the [Orthodox] Church in the East. Things got even worse in 1204, when Western crusaders attacked and looted Constantinople.

This division, called the Great Schism, still exists today. But there is good news: in 1965, Pope Paul VI and Patriarch Athenagoras met, hugged each other, and cancelled the excommunications of 1054. Today, Catholics and Orthodox talk and pray together as friends.

title: The Crusades
text:
In the 600s, a new religion called [Islam] was born in Arabia. Within a hundred years, Muslim armies had conquered the Middle East, North Africa and Spain, including Jerusalem and the Holy Land, where Jesus had lived. For a long time, Christian pilgrims could still visit Jerusalem.

In the 1000s, a new Muslim people, the Seljuk Turks, took over the region and threatened the Byzantine Empire. The Byzantine emperor asked the Pope for help.

In the year 1095, in the French town of Clermont, Pope Urban II gave a big speech. He called on the knights of Europe to go and help the Eastern Christians and to take back Jerusalem. The crowd shouted: "God wills it!" The fighters sewed a cross on their clothes, so they were called "crusaders", from the Latin word "crux" for cross.

Thousands of people set off: knights in armour, but also poor peasants, women and children, who had no idea how far away Jerusalem was! Many died on the way from hunger, disease and battles.

In 1099, after a long and difficult journey, the crusaders captured Jerusalem. Sadly, they massacred many of the inhabitants, Muslims and Jews. This was a terrible crime, and completely against the teaching of Jesus.

The crusaders founded kingdoms in the Holy Land. Special groups of knight-monks were created to protect pilgrims, like the [Knights Templar] and the [Hospitallers], who also ran hospitals.

There were many more Crusades over the next 200 years. The famous Muslim leader Saladin took back Jerusalem in 1187. In the end, the crusaders lost all their kingdoms in 1291.

Today, historians and Christians look at the Crusades with mixed feelings. Some people fought out of real faith, but there was also a lot of violence, greed and cruelty. In the year 2000, Pope John Paul II asked forgiveness for the violence committed by Christians in the past.

On the other hand, there were also peaceful meetings. In 1219, Francis of Assisi crossed the battle lines to talk in peace with the Sultan of Egypt. You will meet him soon!

title: The age of the great cathedrals
text:
In the 1100s, Europe was more peaceful and richer than before. Towns were growing. And people started building incredible churches: the [cathedrals].

A cathedral is the main church of a city, where the bishop has his seat. The word comes from "cathedra", which means "chair" in Latin.

In the year 1163, in Paris, the first stone of a new cathedral was laid: [Notre-Dame de Paris], which means "Our Lady of Paris", in honour of Mary, the mother of Jesus. It took almost 200 years to finish! Most of the people who started building it never saw it completed.

These cathedrals were built in a new style called [Gothic]. The builders invented clever tricks to make the walls higher and thinner:
- pointed arches instead of round ones,
- ribbed [vaults] on the ceiling,
- and [flying buttresses], stone arms outside the building that hold up the walls, like crutches.

Thanks to this, the walls could be filled with huge windows made of [stained glass], pieces of coloured glass assembled like a puzzle. The windows told stories from the Bible in pictures, because most people could not read. They were like a giant comic book made of light! The round windows are called rose windows.

Building a cathedral was the work of a whole city: architects, stonemasons, carpenters, glassmakers, sculptors... Sometimes rich and poor people joined in to pull the carts of stones.

On the outside, you can see funny stone creatures called [gargoyles]. They are actually gutters: when it rains, water comes out of their mouths!

Other famous Gothic cathedrals include Chartres, Reims and Amiens in France, Cologne in Germany, and Canterbury and Salisbury in England.

On the 15th of April 2019, a big fire destroyed the roof and the spire of Notre-Dame de Paris. The whole world was sad. Thousands of craftspeople worked for five years to rebuild it, using the same techniques as in the Middle Ages. It reopened in December 2024, as beautiful as ever!

title: Francis of Assisi, the poor little brother
text:
Francis was born in 1181 in Assisi, a town in Italy. His father was a rich cloth merchant. As a young man, Francis loved parties, beautiful clothes and dreamed of becoming a famous knight.

He went to war, but was captured and spent a year in prison. Then he got very sick. When he came back home, he was different. He started to think about the meaning of his life.

One day, he met a man with [leprosy], a terrible disease. Everybody was scared of lepers and kept away from them. Francis was disgusted too, but he got off his horse, gave the man money and kissed his hand. Later he said this was the moment his life changed.

Another day, in a little ruined chapel called San Damiano, he heard Jesus speaking to him from the cross: "Francis, go and repair my house, which is falling into ruin!" Francis took it literally and started repairing the chapel with stones. Later he understood that God meant the whole Church.

To pay for the repairs, he sold some of his father's cloth. His father was furious and took him to the bishop. In front of the whole town, Francis took off all his clothes, gave them back to his father and said: "From now on, my only father is God in heaven!" The bishop covered him with his own cloak.

Francis started to live in total poverty, begging for food and helping the poor. Others joined him. In 1209, the Pope approved their way of life. They were called the [Franciscans], or the "little brothers" ([friars]). A young woman, [Clare], joined him and founded an order for women: the Poor Clares.

Francis loved nature. He called the sun his "brother", the moon his "sister", and he wrote a famous song about it, "The Canticle of the Sun". The legends say he preached to the birds and tamed a fierce wolf that was scaring the town of Gubbio.

In 1223, he made the first living nativity scene, with a real ox and donkey. That's where the tradition of the Christmas crib comes from!

Francis is the patron saint of animals and ecology.

title: Thomas Aquinas and the first universities
text:
In the 1100s and 1200s, something new appeared in Europe: the [universities]. The first ones were in Bologna (Italy), Paris (France) and Oxford (England). They grew out of the schools of the cathedrals and were run by the Church.

Students came from all over Europe. They all spoke Latin, so a student from Poland could study in Paris without a problem! They studied grammar, logic, arithmetic, music, astronomy... and the most important subject of all, [theology], the study of God.

The most famous teacher of the Middle Ages was Thomas Aquinas. He was born in 1225 near Naples, in Italy, into a noble family. His parents wanted him to become the abbot of the rich monastery of Monte Cassino. But Thomas wanted to join the [Dominicans], a new group of poor preaching friars founded by Saint Dominic.

His family was so angry that his brothers kidnapped him and locked him in the family castle for a whole year! But Thomas didn't give up. He spent his time reading and studying. Finally, his mother helped him escape through a window.

Thomas was big, quiet and calm. In Paris, his classmates made fun of him and called him "the Dumb Ox". But his teacher, Albert the Great, said: "You call him the dumb ox, but one day his bellowing will be heard all over the world!"

At that time, Europeans had rediscovered the books of the Greek philosopher [Aristotle], thanks to translations by Arab and Jewish scholars. Some Christians were worried that his ideas were dangerous. Thomas said: no! Faith and reason are friends. Our intelligence is a gift from God, and we can use it to understand the world and even to think about God.

His biggest book, the Summa Theologica, has 3,000 pages! It tries to answer every question about God and humans, like: "Does God exist?", "What are angels?", "What is happiness?"

Near the end of his life, Thomas had a mystical experience during Mass. After that, he stopped writing. He said: "Everything I have written seems like straw compared to what I have seen." He died in 1274.

title: Joan of Arc, the girl who saved France
text:
In the 1400s, France and England had been at war for almost a hundred years. It is called the [Hundred Years' War]. The English controlled a big part of France, and the French prince, Charles, had not even been crowned king.

In a small village called Domrémy, in eastern France, there lived a peasant girl named Joan. She could not read or write. She looked after animals and helped her mother.

When she was 13, Joan started hearing voices. She said they were saints: Saint Michael the archangel, Saint Catherine and Saint Margaret. They told her to be good and to pray. Later, they told her something unbelievable: "Go and save France, and bring the prince to Reims to be crowned!"

In 1429, when she was 17, Joan convinced a local captain to take her to see the prince. She cut her hair short, dressed like a boy, and rode across the country. The prince hid among his courtiers to test her, but Joan recognized him immediately!

After theologians questioned her, the prince gave her armour, a white banner and a small army. Joan went to the city of Orléans, which had been surrounded by the English for months. In just nine days, the French broke the [siege]! Joan was wounded by an arrow but kept fighting.

Then she led the prince to Reims, where he was crowned King Charles VII in the cathedral, just like the kings before him since Clovis.

But in 1430, Joan was captured and sold to the English. They put her on trial for [heresy] (having wrong beliefs) and for wearing men's clothes. The judges were churchmen who were on the English side. They tried to trick her with difficult questions. When they asked her if she was in God's grace, she answered cleverly: "If I am not, may God put me there; if I am, may God keep me there."

In 1431, Joan was burned alive in Rouen. She was 19 years old.

Twenty-five years later, a new trial declared her innocent. In 1920, the Catholic Church declared her a [saint]. She is one of the patron saints of France.

title: The fall of Constantinople
text:
For more than 1,100 years, [Constantinople] had been the capital of the Eastern Roman Empire, the Byzantine Empire. It was protected by the strongest walls in the world: a triple wall with a moat, and 96 towers.

But by the 1400s, the Byzantine Empire had become very small and weak. Around it, a powerful new Muslim empire had grown: the [Ottoman Empire] of the Turks.

In 1453, the young sultan Mehmed II, only 21 years old, decided to take the city. He brought an army of about 80,000 soldiers, and something new and terrifying: gigantic [cannons]. One of them was 8 metres long and could fire stone balls weighing 500 kilos!

Inside the city, the last emperor, Constantine XI, had only about 7,000 defenders. Still, they fought bravely for almost two months. They had even stretched a huge iron chain across the harbour, called the Golden Horn, so that enemy ships couldn't enter.

But Mehmed had a clever idea: he had his ships pulled over land, on greased wooden logs, over a hill, to put them inside the harbour, behind the chain!

On the 29th of May 1453, the Ottoman army made its final attack and entered the city. The last emperor died fighting. The Byzantine Empire, the last piece of the Roman Empire, was over.

Mehmed rode to the great church of Hagia Sophia and turned it into a [mosque]. Constantinople became the capital of the Ottoman Empire. Today we know it as Istanbul.

This was a huge shock for Christians everywhere. The Orthodox Church continued to exist under Ottoman rule, and the Patriarch still lives in Istanbul today. But after that, the city of Moscow began to see itself as the new centre of Orthodox Christianity, calling itself "the Third Rome".

Many Greek scholars escaped to Italy, bringing precious ancient books with them. This helped the [Renaissance], a big rebirth of art and learning in Europe. Some historians say that 1453 marks the end of the Middle Ages.

title: Gutenberg prints the Bible
text:
Remember the monks who copied books by hand? It took a long time, so books were very rare and very expensive. A Bible could cost as much as a house! Only rich people, churches and monasteries could have one.

Then, around the year 1450, a German goldsmith named Johannes Gutenberg, from the city of Mainz, had a brilliant idea that changed the world.

He created small metal letters, one for each letter of the alphabet, called [movable type]. You could arrange them to make words and pages, put ink on them, and press a sheet of paper on top with a machine: the [printing press]. He got the idea for the press from the machines used to squeeze grapes to make wine! After printing, you could take the letters apart and use them again for another page.

Gutenberg also invented a special ink, oily enough to stick to metal, and a way to make thousands of identical letters quickly.

The first big book he printed, around 1455, was... the Bible! In Latin. It is called the Gutenberg Bible. It had 1,286 pages, in two columns, and it was so beautiful that people thought it had been written by hand. About 180 copies were printed. Today, only 49 are left, and they are among the most valuable books in the world.

Poor Gutenberg did not become rich. He had borrowed money for his invention, and his business partner took his workshop away from him!

But his invention spread like wildfire. By the year 1500, there were printing shops in over 250 European cities, and around 20 million books had been printed!

For Christianity, this was a revolution. Now, the Bible could be printed in large numbers, and soon in the languages that ordinary people spoke. People could read the Bible for themselves, at home. New ideas could spread very fast through printed books and leaflets.

Without the printing press, the big events of the next pins, like the Reformation, might never have happened!

title: Christianity crosses the ocean to the Americas
text:
In 1492, Christopher Columbus crossed the Atlantic Ocean and arrived in the Americas. The Europeans called it the "New World", but of course, millions of people were already living there, with their own cultures, cities and religions: the Aztecs, the Maya, the Incas and many others.

The kings of Spain and Portugal wanted to conquer these lands and find gold. They also wanted to spread Christianity. So on their ships, along with soldiers, there were priests and monks, called [missionaries].

This is one of the darkest chapters in the history of Christianity. The [conquistadors] (the conquerors) were often very cruel. They took the land, forced the native people to work like slaves, and destroyed their temples. Millions of native Americans died, from wars, hard work, and above all from new diseases brought by the Europeans, like smallpox.

But some Christians stood up against this injustice. The most famous was Bartolomé de las Casas. He came to the Americas as a young colonist and owned native slaves himself. But one day, while preparing a sermon, he read a passage in the Bible that made him realize this was wrong.

He freed his slaves, became a Dominican friar and spent 50 years defending the native people. He crossed the ocean many times to argue with the King of Spain. He wrote that the native Americans were human beings with the same dignity as Europeans, created by God, and that nobody had the right to enslave them. He was called the "Protector of the Indians".

In 1531, in Mexico, a native man named Juan Diego said that Mary, the mother of Jesus, had appeared to him on a hill. She spoke to him in his own language, Nahuatl, and looked like a native woman. The image of Our Lady of Guadalupe on his cloak became the symbol of Mexican Christianity. Today, it is one of the most visited Christian shrines in the world.

Today, about 40% of all the Catholics in the world live in Latin America!

title: Michelangelo paints the Sistine Chapel
text:
Around 1500, Italy was living a golden age of art and learning called the [Renaissance], which means "rebirth". Artists rediscovered the beauty of ancient Greek and Roman art, and created amazing masterpieces, many of them about Christian stories.

In Rome, the popes wanted to make their city the most beautiful in the world. In 1508, Pope Julius II asked a sculptor named Michelangelo to paint the ceiling of the Sistine Chapel, the Pope's private chapel in the Vatican.

Michelangelo was not happy! He said: "I am a sculptor, not a painter!" He thought his rivals had set a trap to make him fail. But you couldn't say no to Pope Julius, who was nicknamed "the Terrible Pope"!

The ceiling is huge: about 40 metres long and 13 metres wide, 20 metres above the floor. Michelangelo built a special wooden platform, a [scaffolding], and painted standing up, with his head tilted backwards and his arm raised above him, for four years! Paint dripped into his eyes. He wrote a funny poem complaining that his beard pointed to heaven and his back was bent like a bow.

He painted using a technique called [fresco]: painting on wet plaster, so the colours become part of the wall. He had to work fast before the plaster dried!

The result is one of the greatest works of art ever made. There are more than 300 figures telling stories from the book of [Genesis]: the creation of the world, Adam and Eve, Noah and the flood. The most famous scene is "The Creation of Adam", where God reaches out his finger to give life to the first man. Their fingers almost touch.

Twenty years later, Michelangelo came back and painted "The Last Judgement" on the wall behind the altar.

Michelangelo also sculpted the "Pietà" (Mary holding Jesus after his death) and designed the huge dome of Saint Peter's Basilica.

Today, the Sistine Chapel is also the place where the [cardinals] meet to elect a new pope, in a meeting called a [conclave].

title: Martin Luther and the 95 Theses
text:
Martin Luther was born in Germany in 1483. His father wanted him to become a lawyer. But one day, when he was 21, Luther was caught in a terrible thunderstorm. A lightning bolt struck the ground right next to him! Terrified, he cried out: "Saint Anne, help me! I will become a monk!" And he kept his promise.

Luther was a very serious monk, but he was always worried. He was afraid that he was not good enough for God and that he would go to hell, no matter how hard he tried.

He became a professor of the Bible in the town of Wittenberg. By studying Paul's letters, he discovered something that gave him great peace: we cannot earn God's love by our good works. God gives his forgiveness freely, as a gift, to those who trust him. This is called "[justification by faith]".

At that time, the Church was selling "[indulgences]". People were told that if they paid money, they or their dead relatives would spend less time in [purgatory], a place of purification after death. The money was used, among other things, to build the new Saint Peter's Basilica in Rome. A preacher named Tetzel even had a little slogan: "As soon as the coin in the box rings, the soul from purgatory springs!"

Luther was furious. On the 31st of October 1517, according to tradition, he nailed a list of 95 arguments, called the "95 Theses", on the door of the church in Wittenberg, inviting people to debate.

Thanks to the printing press, his theses were copied and spread all over Germany in just two weeks! It was like a message going viral.

The Pope asked Luther to take back his words. He refused. In 1521, in front of the emperor, he said: "Here I stand, I can do no other. God help me." He was declared an outlaw. A friendly prince hid him in the Wartburg castle, where Luther translated the New Testament into German in just 11 weeks.

This was the beginning of the [Reformation], and of the [Protestant] churches. Today, the 31st of October is Reformation Day.

title: Henry VIII and the Church of England
text:
In England, the Reformation happened in a very unusual way: because of a king who wanted a new wife!

[Henry VIII] became king of England in 1509. At first, he was a very good Catholic. He even wrote a book against Martin Luther, and the Pope gave him the title "Defender of the Faith".

Henry was married to Catherine of Aragon, a Spanish princess. They had a daughter, Mary, but no son. Henry desperately wanted a son to become king after him. He also fell in love with a young lady of the court, Anne Boleyn.

So Henry asked the Pope to cancel his marriage with Catherine. The Pope said no. (He was also under pressure from Catherine's nephew, the powerful emperor Charles V!)

Henry was furious. In 1534, he made Parliament pass a law called the Act of Supremacy. It declared that the king, not the Pope, was the head of the Church in England. This is how the Church of England, also called the [Anglican] Church, was born.

Anyone who refused to accept this was in danger. Henry's friend, the wise [Thomas More], refused, and was executed. He said: "I die the king's good servant, but God's first."

Henry closed all the monasteries in England, took their lands and treasures, and sold them. Many beautiful abbeys became ruins that you can still visit today.

Meanwhile, a scholar named [William Tyndale] had translated the Bible into English, so that "even a boy who drives the plough" could read it. At that time, it was forbidden, and Tyndale was executed in 1536. But just a few years later, Henry ordered an English Bible to be placed in every church!

Henry had six wives. English children learn a rhyme to remember what happened to them: "Divorced, beheaded, died; divorced, beheaded, survived."

After Henry, England went back and forth between Protestant and Catholic, until Queen Elizabeth I found a middle way. Today, the Anglican Communion has about 85 million members around the world.

title: John Calvin in Geneva
text:
John Calvin was born in 1509 in Noyon, in the north of France. He was a very bright student who studied law and ancient languages in Paris. Around the age of 24, he read the books of Luther and other reformers and became a Protestant.

At that time, in France, it was dangerous to be a Protestant. Calvin had to escape. He went to Basel, in Switzerland, where, at only 26 years old, he wrote a famous book explaining the Protestant faith very clearly: the "Institutes of the Christian Religion".

In 1536, he was passing through the city of Geneva, planning to stay just one night. But a local preacher, William Farel, begged him to stay and help. When Calvin refused, Farel threatened that God would curse his studies if he left! So Calvin stayed.

It didn't go smoothly: the people of Geneva found him too strict, and they threw him out in 1538! But in 1541, they asked him to come back, and this time he stayed for the rest of his life.

Calvin wanted to make Geneva a model Christian city. There were strict rules: no dancing, no card games, no fancy clothes, everyone had to go to church. Some people found it too harsh. But Geneva also became a city famous for its schools, its university, and its help for the poor and for refugees.

Thousands of Protestants who were persecuted in France, England, Italy and elsewhere came to live in Geneva. They were trained there and brought Calvin's ideas back home.

Calvin's churches are called "[Reformed]" churches. In France, Calvinists were called [Huguenots]. In Scotland, John Knox created the [Presbyterian] Church. In the Netherlands too, Calvin's ideas were very popular.

Calvinist churches are very simple: no statues, no paintings, no candles. The most important thing is the Bible, read and explained by the pastor, and the singing of the Psalms by the whole congregation.

Today, you can see the huge "Reformation Wall" in a park in Geneva, with statues of Calvin, Farel, Knox and others, and the city's motto: "After darkness, light".

title: The Council of Trent and the Jesuits
text:
The Protestant Reformation was a huge shock for the Catholic Church. In a few years, it had lost half of Europe! The Church realized it had to react and improve itself. This period is called the [Catholic Reformation] or the Counter-Reformation.

The Pope called a big meeting of bishops in the town of [Trent], in northern Italy. The Council of Trent lasted, with long breaks, for 18 years, from 1545 to 1563!

The Council did two things:
- First, it clearly explained Catholic beliefs where Protestants disagreed: the importance of the Church's tradition as well as the Bible, the seven [sacraments], the Mass, the saints, and purgatory.
- Second, it fixed many problems that the Protestants had rightly criticized. It forbade the selling of indulgences. It demanded that bishops live in their cities and take care of their people. It created special schools, called [seminaries], to train priests properly.

At the same time, new religious groups were born. The most famous was founded by a Spanish soldier, Ignatius of Loyola.

In 1521, Ignatius was badly wounded by a cannonball in a battle. While recovering in bed, he was bored and asked for adventure novels. But the only books in the house were a life of Jesus and a book about the saints! Reading them, he thought: "Saint Francis did this, so I can do it too!" His life changed.

With a few friends from the university of Paris, including Francis Xavier, he founded the [Society of Jesus] in 1540. Its members are called [Jesuits]. They were like the "special forces" of the Church, ready to go anywhere in the world where the Pope sent them.

The Jesuits founded hundreds of schools and universities, which were among the best in Europe. They also became great missionaries, explorers and scientists.

The Catholic Reformation also gave the world a new style of art: the [Baroque], full of movement, gold, light and emotion, to touch people's hearts.

title: Francis Xavier in Japan, Matteo Ricci in China
text:
In the 1500s, European ships sailed all the way to Asia, and missionaries went with them. Two Jesuits became especially famous.

Francis Xavier was one of Ignatius of Loyola's first friends. In 1541, he left Europe and never came back. He travelled to India, to today's Indonesia, and then, in 1549, he became one of the first Europeans to reach Japan!

He was amazed by the Japanese people. He wrote that they were "the best people discovered so far". At first, he made many mistakes, because he didn't know the language or the customs. He arrived wearing old, poor clothes, and people didn't take him seriously. So he learned to dress properly and to bring gifts, like a clock and a music box, to the local lords. In two years, he baptized hundreds of people.

In the following decades, around 300,000 Japanese became Christians! But then the rulers of Japan became suspicious of foreigners. In 1597, 26 Christians were crucified in Nagasaki. Christianity was banned. Some Japanese Christians, called the Kakure Kirishitan ("hidden Christians"), secretly kept their faith for 250 years, hiding statues of Mary disguised as the Buddhist goddess Kannon! When missionaries returned in 1865, they were astonished to find them still there.

Francis Xavier died in 1552 on a small island off the coast of China, which he dreamed of entering.

That dream was realized by another Italian Jesuit: Matteo Ricci. He arrived in China in 1582. Instead of trying to change the Chinese, he became Chinese in many ways!
