He learned to speak and write Chinese perfectly, wore the silk robes of a Chinese scholar, and studied the books of the great philosopher [Confucius].

Ricci was also a scientist. He made the first map of the world in Chinese, showing China in the middle to please his hosts! He brought clocks and taught mathematics and astronomy.

In 1601, he became the first European invited into the [Forbidden City] in Beijing, the Emperor's palace. He showed how Christianity could respect a different culture. This is called [inculturation].

title: Wars of religion, and learning to live together
text:
After the Reformation, Europe was divided between Catholics and Protestants. Sadly, instead of talking, they often fought. For more than a hundred years, there were terrible "[wars of religion]".

In France, Catholics fought against Protestants, the [Huguenots], in eight wars between 1562 and 1598. The worst moment was the [Saint Bartholomew's Day massacre], on the 24th of August 1572. In Paris, on the night when many Protestant nobles had come to the city for a royal wedding, Catholics attacked and killed thousands of Protestants. The violence spread to other cities.

The man who ended these wars was [Henry IV]. He was a Protestant prince, but when he became King of France, he converted to Catholicism, because most French people were Catholic. He is supposed to have said: "Paris is well worth a Mass!"

In 1598, Henry IV signed the Edict of Nantes. It allowed Protestants to practise their religion in certain places, gave them the same rights as Catholics, and let them keep some fortified towns for their safety. It was one of the first laws in Europe to allow two Christian religions to live side by side in the same country. This idea is called [tolerance].

Unfortunately, in 1685, his grandson Louis XIV cancelled the Edict. About 200,000 Huguenots fled France to England, the Netherlands, Germany, Switzerland and even South Africa.

In Germany, an even more terrible war broke out: the [Thirty Years' War] (1618–1648). It started as a war between Catholics and Protestants but became a fight between the great powers of Europe. Villages were burned, and in some parts of Germany, one person out of three died.

In 1648, exhausted, the countries signed the [Peace of Westphalia]. Each ruler could choose the religion of his land, and people slowly got used to living next to those who believed differently.

These wars taught Europe a hard lesson: you cannot force people to believe with swords. Today, freedom of religion is considered a basic human right.

title: The King James Bible and the Mayflower Pilgrims
text:
In England, in 1604, King James I gathered 47 scholars and asked them to make a new English translation of the Bible, one that everyone could accept.

They worked in six teams, at Oxford, Cambridge and Westminster, for seven years. They translated directly from the Hebrew and Greek texts. In 1611, the King James Bible was published.

Its language was so beautiful and musical that it deeply shaped the English language. Many everyday expressions come from it, like "a drop in the bucket", "the salt of the earth", "the powers that be" or "a labour of love". For more than 300 years, it was the Bible of almost all English-speaking Protestants, and it is still widely read today.

But not everyone in England was happy with the Church of England. Some Protestants, called [Puritans], wanted a simpler, "purer" Church, without bishops or ceremonies. Some of them, called Separatists, were persecuted and escaped to the Netherlands.

In September 1620, about 100 people, some of them Separatists looking for religious freedom, boarded a small ship called the Mayflower. The journey across the Atlantic took 66 days, in a crowded, wet and smelly ship, through terrible storms. A baby was born on the way, and was named Oceanus!

In November, they landed in America and founded a colony called Plymouth, in today's Massachusetts. They are known as the [Pilgrims] or Pilgrim Fathers. Before landing, they signed an agreement to make fair laws together: the Mayflower Compact.

The first winter was terrible: half of them died of cold, hunger and disease. The native people of the region, the Wampanoag, helped them. A native man named Squanto, who spoke English, taught them how to grow corn and where to fish.

In autumn 1621, after their first harvest, the Pilgrims and the Wampanoag shared a three-day feast. Americans remember it as the first [Thanksgiving].

Many other Christian groups later came to America looking for freedom: Quakers, Catholics, Baptists, Mennonites... That's why religious freedom is so important in the United States.

title: John Wesley and the Great Awakening
text:
In the 1700s, many people in Europe were fascinated by science and reason. This period is called the [Enlightenment]. Some thinkers made fun of religion. In many churches, sermons had become boring, and ordinary people, especially poor workers, rarely went to church.

Then, a new wave of faith came: the "Great Awakening", also called the [revival].

In England, the leader was John Wesley, a priest of the Church of England. When he was a little boy of 5, his family's house caught fire. He was the last one inside, and was rescued at the very last moment by neighbours standing on each other's shoulders at the window! His mother called him "a brand plucked from the burning".

At university in Oxford, John and his brother Charles started a club where students prayed, studied the Bible and visited prisoners, very regularly and methodically. The other students made fun of them and called them "Methodists". The name stuck!

On the 24th of May 1738, at a meeting in London, while someone was reading Luther, John Wesley said he felt his heart "strangely warmed". He felt sure that God loved and forgave him personally.

After that, he travelled all over Britain on horseback, about 400,000 kilometres in his life, that's ten times around the Earth! Because many churches would not let him preach, he preached outdoors: in fields, in markets, and even at the entrance of coal mines, to thousands of workers. Some people threw stones and rotten eggs at him, but he kept going.

His brother, Charles Wesley, wrote more than 6,000 hymns, including "Hark! The Herald Angels Sing", which is still sung at Christmas.

The Methodists also cared about the poor. They opened schools, free clinics and helped people in prison. Wesley said: "Do all the good you can, by all the means you can, in all the ways you can, to all the people you can, as long as ever you can!"

In America, preachers like George Whitefield drew enormous crowds too. Today, there are about 80 million Methodists in the world.

title: Christians against slavery
text:
For centuries, millions of Africans were captured, put on ships and sold as slaves in the Americas. This was the [Atlantic slave trade]. It was one of the greatest crimes in human history. Sadly, many people who called themselves Christians took part in it, and some even used the Bible to defend it.

But other Christians became convinced that slavery was completely against the teaching of Jesus: every human being is created in the image of God and is loved by God. They fought to end it. They were called [abolitionists].

In England, the [Quakers], a small Christian group, were the first to organize against slavery. A famous medallion was made, showing a kneeling African man in chains, with the words: "Am I not a man and a brother?"

A young member of Parliament, William Wilberforce, became a committed Christian in 1785. He decided to dedicate his life to ending the slave trade. Every year, he proposed a law in Parliament. Every year, it was rejected. Many people were getting rich from the slave trade and hated him. He received threats. His health was fragile.

But he never gave up. After 20 years of efforts, in 1807, Parliament finally voted to abolish the slave trade in the British Empire! In 1833, just three days before Wilberforce died, slavery itself was abolished.

The song "[Amazing Grace]" was written by John Newton, a former slave-ship captain who became a Christian minister and later joined the fight against slavery.

In the United States, slavery continued until 1865. Harriet Tubman was born a slave. She escaped, and then went back again and again, about 13 times, to guide around 70 other slaves to freedom, through a secret network called the [Underground Railroad]. She was a deeply Christian woman who said God guided her. People called her "Moses", because like Moses, she led her people out of slavery. She said: "I never lost a single passenger!"

The African American churches, with their [spirituals] (songs of faith and hope), gave slaves strength and courage.

title: Soup, soap and salvation: helping the poor
text:
In the 1800s, the [Industrial Revolution] transformed Europe. Factories appeared everywhere, and millions of people moved from the countryside to the cities to work. But the workers were often very poor. Families lived crammed in dark, dirty houses. Children as young as 6 worked 12 hours a day in factories and mines.

Many Christians decided to do something about it.

In London, a Methodist preacher named William Booth and his wife Catherine Booth started working in 1865 in the poorest area of the city, the East End. They preached in the streets and helped drunkards, homeless people and orphans.

In 1878, they gave their movement a surprising name: The Salvation Army! It was organized like an army, with uniforms, ranks (like captain or general), flags, and brass bands playing in the streets. They were "soldiers" fighting against poverty and sin. Their motto was "Soup, soap and salvation": first give people food, then help them get clean, and then tell them about God's love.

At first, people attacked them in the streets and mocked them. But they kept going. Catherine Booth insisted that women could preach just like men, which was very unusual at the time. Today, the Salvation Army works in more than 130 countries.

In Switzerland, a Christian businessman named Henry Dunant saw the horrible aftermath of a battle in Italy in 1859. Thousands of wounded soldiers were left without care. He organized the local people to help all the wounded, from both sides, saying: "We are all brothers!" In 1863, he founded the [Red Cross]. Its symbol is the Swiss flag with the colours reversed. Dunant received the very first Nobel Peace Prize in 1901.

At the same time, many Christians founded schools, hospitals and orphanages. In England, [Sunday schools] taught working children to read. Dr Barnardo opened homes for thousands of street children. Nurses like [Florence Nightingale] changed medicine.

Many of these organizations still help millions of people today.

title: Azusa Street and the Pentecostal movement
text:
In April 1906, in Los Angeles, in the United States, something happened in an old, run-down building on a street called Azusa Street. It had been a church, then a stable and a warehouse. The floor was covered with sawdust, and the benches were made of planks placed on boxes.

The meetings were led by William J. Seymour, an African American preacher, the son of former slaves. He had only one eye; he had lost the other one to smallpox. Because of racial segregation laws, when he wanted to learn at a Bible school, he had to listen to the lessons sitting in the hallway, outside the classroom!

At Azusa Street, people prayed for hours, sometimes day and night. They said that they were filled with the Holy Spirit, just like the apostles at Pentecost. Some started "[speaking in tongues]", praying in words or languages they didn't know. Others said they were healed. People sang, shouted, danced and cried with joy.

The meetings went on almost every day for three years! Visitors came from all over the United States and even from other countries.

What was really surprising for that time was that Black people, white people, Latinos and Asians, men and women, rich and poor, prayed together side by side. In a country where Black and white people were separated everywhere, a visitor wrote: "The color line was washed away in the blood!"

Some newspapers made fun of them, calling it "a weird babel of tongues". But the movement spread incredibly fast.

This was the beginning of the [Pentecostal] movement, named after the day of Pentecost. Later, a similar movement also appeared inside the older churches, including the Catholic Church, called the "[charismatic] renewal".

Pentecostal churches are known for their joyful worship, with modern music, clapping hands and raised arms, and their strong belief in the gifts of the Holy Spirit.

Today, there are more than 600 million Pentecostal and charismatic Christians in the world, especially in Africa, Latin America and Asia. It is the fastest-growing form of Christianity!

title: Courage in dark times: Bonhoeffer and Kolbe
text:
In 1933, [Adolf Hitler] and his [Nazi] party took power in Germany. They were racist and violent, and they especially hated the Jews. They wanted everyone, including the churches, to obey Hitler completely.

Some Christians went along with the Nazis, and some even supported them. But others resisted, sometimes at the cost of their lives.

Dietrich Bonhoeffer was a young German Lutheran pastor and teacher. He had studied in New York, where he loved going to a Black church in Harlem, and he saw how unfair racism was. When the Nazis came to power, he immediately spoke out against them. Two days after Hitler became chancellor, Bonhoeffer criticized him on the radio, and his speech was cut off!

He helped create the Confessing Church, Protestant Christians who refused to let the Nazis control the Church. He said: "Silence in the face of evil is itself evil."

In 1939, he was safe in America, but he decided to go back to Germany. He said he could not help rebuild his country after the war if he did not share its suffering. He joined a secret group trying to stop Hitler and helped Jews escape to Switzerland. He was arrested in 1943 and executed in April 1945, just two weeks before the end of the war. His last words were: "This is the end, but for me, the beginning of life."

Maximilian Kolbe was a Polish Catholic priest, a Franciscan. During the war, his monastery hid about 2,000 refugees, including many Jews. He was arrested and sent to the terrible [concentration camp] of Auschwitz.

One day in 1941, a prisoner escaped. To punish the others, the guards chose ten men to die of hunger. One of them cried: "My wife! My children!" Father Kolbe stepped forward and said: "I am a Catholic priest. Let me take his place." The guards accepted. Kolbe died, and the man he saved, Franciszek Gajowniczek, survived the war and lived to be 93.

Many ordinary Christians also risked their lives to hide Jewish families. Israel honours them with the title "[Righteous Among the Nations]".

title: The Second Vatican Council opens the windows
text:
In 1958, the cardinals elected a new pope: Angelo Roncalli, who took the name [John XXIII]. He was 76 years old. Many people thought he would be a quiet "temporary" pope who wouldn't change much. They were very wrong!

John XXIII was the son of poor farmers, cheerful and full of humour. He visited children in hospitals and prisoners in jail. Once, someone asked him how many people worked in the Vatican. He answered: "About half of them!"

Only three months after being elected, he surprised everyone by announcing a [council], a huge meeting of all the Catholic bishops of the world. When asked why, legend says he opened a window and said: "I want to throw open the windows of the Church, so that we can see out and the people can see in!" He called it "[aggiornamento]", an Italian word meaning "bringing up to date".

The Second Vatican Council opened in October 1962 in Saint Peter's Basilica. More than 2,500 bishops came from every continent. It was the biggest meeting in the history of the Church! Protestant and Orthodox observers were invited too, which had never happened before.

John XXIII died in 1963, but his successor, [Paul VI], continued the council until 1965.

The council made many important changes:
- Mass could now be said in the local language, instead of only in Latin, so that everybody could understand.
- The priest now faced the people during Mass.
- Catholics were encouraged to read the Bible.
- The Church said it wanted friendship and dialogue with other Christians. This is called [ecumenism].
- It declared that people must be free to choose their religion, without force.
- It expressed deep respect for other religions, especially for the Jewish people, and rejected the old, false idea that the Jews were guilty of Jesus' death.
- It said that all Christians, not only priests and nuns, are called to be holy.

For many Catholics, it felt like a breath of fresh air. Almost everything you see today at a Catholic Mass comes from this council.

title: Martin Luther King Jr.: "I have a dream"
text:
Even after slavery ended in the United States, Black Americans did not have the same rights as white people, especially in the southern states. By law, they had to use separate schools, separate restaurants, separate drinking fountains, and sit at the back of buses. This was called [segregation].

Martin Luther King Jr. was born in 1929 in Atlanta. His father was a Baptist pastor, and Martin became a pastor too. He was named after... Martin Luther!

In 1955, in the city of Montgomery, a Black woman named Rosa Parks refused to give up her seat on a bus to a white man. She was arrested. Martin Luther King, then only 26 years old, led a boycott: for more than a year, Black people refused to take the buses, walking kilometres to work every day. In the end, the courts said that bus segregation was illegal. They had won!

King's big idea was [nonviolence]. He took it from Jesus' words "Love your enemies" and from the Indian leader [Gandhi]. He said: "Darkness cannot drive out darkness; only light can do that. Hate cannot drive out hate; only love can do that."

He and his friends organized marches and sit-ins. They were attacked by police dogs and water cannons, and King was put in prison about 30 times. His house was bombed. But he always asked his followers not to hit back.

On the 28th of August 1963, 250,000 people gathered in Washington, D.C. King gave one of the most famous speeches in history. He said: "I have a dream that my four little children will one day live in a nation where they will not be judged by the colour of their skin, but by the content of their character."

In 1964, the United States passed the Civil Rights Act, ending legal segregation. The same year, King received the Nobel Peace Prize, at 35.

On the 4th of April 1968, Martin Luther King was murdered. He was 39. Today, the United States honours him with a national holiday every January.

title: Mother Teresa, the saint of the poorest
text:
Mother Teresa's real name was Agnes Gonxha Bojaxhiu. She was born in 1910 in Skopje (today in North Macedonia), in an Albanian family. When she was 12, she already felt that God was calling her to be a missionary.

At 18, she left her family forever and became a nun with the Sisters of Loreto. They sent her to India, where she taught geography and history in a school for girls in the city of Calcutta (today called [Kolkata]) for almost 20 years.

On the way to school, she saw the terrible poverty in the streets. Thousands of people lived and died on the pavement, with nobody to care for them.

In 1946, on a train, she felt what she called "a call within a call": God was asking her to leave her school and serve "the poorest of the poor". So in 1948, she took off her nun's habit and put on a simple white Indian [sari] with a blue border, the clothes of poor Indian women. She went into the slums, with no money, and started teaching children under a tree, writing letters in the dirt with a stick.

Some of her former students joined her. In 1950, she founded a new group of nuns: the Missionaries of Charity.

In 1952, she opened a home for dying people, where people found in the streets could die in peace, with dignity, surrounded by love. She said: "They lived like animals, but they die like angels." Then she opened homes for lepers, orphans and sick people.

She once said: "Not all of us can do great things. But we can do small things with great love." And: "Peace begins with a smile."

In 1979, Mother Teresa received the [Nobel Peace Prize]. She asked that the usual gala dinner be cancelled, and the money be given to the poor!

She died in 1997. Today, her Missionaries of Charity, with their white and blue saris, work in more than 130 countries. In 2016, the Catholic Church declared her a saint: Saint Teresa of Calcutta.

title: Christianity today: a worldwide family
text:
Here we are, 2,000 years after Jesus! What does Christianity look like today?

There are about 2.4 billion Christians in the world. That's almost one person out of three! It is the largest religion on Earth.

But Christianity has changed a lot. In 1900, most Christians lived in Europe and North America. Today, most Christians live in Africa, Latin America and Asia. The country with the most Christians is the United States, followed by Brazil and Mexico. Nigeria, Congo, the Philippines and Ethiopia also have huge numbers of Christians. A typical Christian today is more likely to be a young African woman than an old European man!

In Europe, fewer people go to church than before, while in Africa and Asia, churches are often packed.

Christians belong to many different families, called [denominations]:
- Catholics, about half of all Christians, led by the Pope in Rome,
- Protestants, including Lutherans, Reformed, Anglicans, Baptists, Methodists, Pentecostals and many others,
- Orthodox Christians, mostly in Eastern Europe, Russia, Greece and the Middle East,
- and ancient Eastern churches, like the [Copts] of Egypt and the Ethiopian Church.

They have their differences, but they share the essential: faith in Jesus Christ, the Bible, baptism, and the command to love God and their neighbour. More and more, they work and pray together.

In 2013, [Pope Francis], from Argentina, became the first pope from the Americas. He asked Christians to care for the poor, for migrants and for our planet, "our common home". He died on Easter Monday 2025.

In May 2025, the cardinals elected Pope Leo XIV, born in Chicago, the first pope from the United States. He had worked for many years as a missionary in Peru.

In some countries, Christians are still persecuted for their faith, just like in the time of the Roman Empire.

The story isn't finished! Christians believe that every person, including you, can write the next page, with kindness, courage and love. What would you like to add to this timeline?
